subject: Comparing effects from two different models

messages.author: 63c84d34940e15df
messages.subject: Comparing effects from two different models
parts:
I am using lavaan to compare predictors of the same DV. I have two models:
modelNoAtt <- 'pursuit ~ a*IAT + b*explicit
        # difference effect
        diff := a - b'
modelAtt <- 'pursuit ~ a*IAT + b*explicit + c*attitude
        # difference effect
        diff := a - b'

[pursuit, IAT, explicit, and attitude are the variables in my dataset]

When I use sem to fit those models, the diff effect is significant in modelNoAtt but not in modelAtt. 

What I want to know is whether the diff effect in modelNoAtt is significantly larger than the diff effect in modelAtt. 
In more abstract terms, I want to examine whether when we control for the variable 'attitude', the advantage of IAT over explicit in predicting pursuit becomes significantly smaller. 

Thanks

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Comparing effects from two different models
parts:
What I want to know is whether the diff effect in modelNoAtt is significantly larger than the diff effect in modelAtt. 
In more abstract terms, I want to examine whether when we control for the variable 'attitude', the advantage of IAT over explicit in predicting pursuit becomes significantly smaller.

You could refit model modelNoAtt with the constraint a == the point estimate of a in modelAtt.  But that would treat the estimate in modelAtt as a known value rather than an estimate with a sampling distribution (i.e., you would be pretending that the SE of a in modelAtt is zero), so I wouldn't recommend that.  Instead, you could use a Monte Carlo approach (described here for the case of mediation: http://quantpsy.org/medmc/medmc.htm) by drawing both values from their estimated sampling distributions (assumed normal with MLE, or OLS in your case because it is just a univariate regression model), then calculating the differences for each draw to get an empirical distribution of the differences.

## draw 10,000 values from the distribution of a under the first model
a.without.c <- rnorm(10000, mean = coef(modelNoAtt)["a"], sd = sqrt(vcov(modelNoAtt)["a","a"]))
## draw 10,000 values from the distribution of a under the second model
a.with.c <- rnorm(10000, mean = coef(modelAtt)["a"], sd = sqrt(vcov(modelAtt)["a","a"]))
## calculate differences
a.diff <- a.without.c
## calculate 95% CI for true difference, test whether null hypothesis (zero) is in the CI
quantile(a.diff, probs = c(.025, .975))

This takes into account the uncertainty in both estimates of "a", but it implicitly assumes that those two estimates are unrelated (correlation == 0), which is certainly not true.  I can't think of a way to estimate the correlation between estimates of models from 2 different model fits, but you could try out a whole range of them (say, from -0.9 to 0.9 in increments of 0.1) as a sort of sensitivity analysis, to see under what conditions the difference in "a" is significant (perhaps all, perhaps none, so you could try the extremes first).  Look into the mvrnorm() function in the MASS package for random multivariate-normal draws.

I'm not even sure about the validity of the test you want to perform, so you might want to post your question on SEMNET and see if any more informed researchers have better advice:

http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.author: 63c84d34940e15df
messages.subject: Re: Comparing effects from two different models
parts:
Thank you, Alex. 

Based on your suggestion I tried the following code:
library(semTools)
modelNoAtt <- 'pursuit ~ a*IAT + b*explicit'
fitNoAtt <- sem(modelNoAtt, data = data)

vcov(fitNoAtt)
#Based on the output from vcov
ACNoAtt <- matrix(c(0.011,-0.001,
               -0.001,0.003), nrow=2, byrow=TRUE)
medNoAtt <- 'a + b*-1'
aParamNoAtt <- fitNoAtt@ParTable$est[1]
bParamNoAtt <- fitNoAtt@ParTable$est[2]
monteCarloMed(medNoAtt, coef1=aParamNoAtt, coef2=bParamNoAtt, outputValues=FALSE, plot=TRUE, ACM=ACNoAtt)

modelAtt <- 'pursuit ~ a*IAT + b*explicit + c*attitude'
fitAtt <- sem(modelAtt, data = data)
vcov(fitAtt)
#Based on the output from vcov
ACAtt <- matrix(c(0.006,0,
                    0,0.002), nrow=2, byrow=TRUE)
medAtt <- 'a + b*-1'
aParamAtt <- fitAtt@ParTable$est[1]
bParamAtt <- fitAtt@ParTable$est[2]
monteCarloMed(medAtt, coef1=aParamAtt, coef2=bParamAtt, outputValues=FALSE, plot=TRUE, ACM=ACAtt)

I obtained the following results:
$`Point Estimate`
[1] 0.4532665

$`95% Confidence Interval`
         
LL 0.2126
UL 0.7005

Second model:
$`Point Estimate`
[1] 0.1518568

$`95% Confidence Interval`
          
LL -0.0214
UL  0.3271

a) I wonder whether there is something fundamentally wrong in this analysis strategy that jumps out to anyone. 
Especially, does it seem fine to request a distribution of the effect 'a-b' with the notation 'a+b*-1'?

b) Excuse my ignorance, but from these two overlapping confidence intervals, how can I infer whether the two effects are significantly different?

messages.author: 5d4f9e7f97c21008
messages.subject: Re: Comparing effects from two different models
parts:
That all looks fine to me. monteCarloMed will evaluate any expression given (assume it is a legitimate expression that yields a numeric answer). So either a+b*-1 or a-b will work. 

To compare the two effects you could use a Monte Carlo Confidence interval comparing the difference between differences. The expression would be something like: (a1-b1)-(a2-b2)   and you'd have to pull the estimates and ACM from both models (for the ACM, any elements of the ACM representing the covariance between paramters from different models, e.g. cov(a1,a2) would be set to 0).

On Wednesday, August 24, 2016 at 4:11:27 PM UTC+3, Alex Schoemann wrote:
To piggyback on Terry's suggestion for a Monte Carlo confidence interval. The function MonteCarloMed in the semTools package allows for the creation of Monte Carlo confidence intervals for any (user specified) combination of parameters.

On Wednesday, August 24, 2016 at 5:08:52 AM UTC-4, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
What I want to know is whether the diff effect in modelNoAtt is significantly larger than the diff effect in modelAtt. 
In more abstract terms, I want to examine whether when we control for the variable 'attitude', the advantage of IAT over explicit in predicting pursuit becomes significantly smaller. 

You could refit model modelNoAtt with the constraint a == the point estimate of a in modelAtt.  But that would treat the estimate in modelAtt as a known value rather than an estimate with a sampling distribution (i.e., you would be pretending that the SE of a in modelAtt is zero), so I wouldn't recommend that.  Instead, you could use a Monte Carlo approach (described here for the case of mediation: http://quantpsy.org/medmc/medmc.htm) by drawing both values from their estimated sampling distributions (assumed normal with MLE, or OLS in your case because it is just a univariate regression model), then calculating the differences for each draw to get an empirical distribution of the differences.

## draw 10,000 values from the distribution of a under the first model
a.without.c <- rnorm(10000, mean = coef(modelNoAtt)["a"], sd = sqrt(vcov(modelNoAtt)["a","a"]))
## draw 10,000 values from the distribution of a under the second model
a.with.c <- rnorm(10000, mean = coef(modelAtt)["a"], sd = sqrt(vcov(modelAtt)["a","a"]))
## calculate differences
a.diff <- a.without.c
## calculate 95% CI for true difference, test whether null hypothesis (zero) is in the CI
quantile(a.diff, probs = c(.025, .975))

This takes into account the uncertainty in both estimates of "a", but it implicitly assumes that those two estimates are unrelated (correlation == 0), which is certainly not true.  I can't think of a way to estimate the correlation between estimates of models from 2 different model fits, but you could try out a whole range of them (say, from -0.9 to 0.9 in increments of 0.1) as a sort of sensitivity analysis, to see under what conditions the difference in "a" is significant (perhaps all, perhaps none, so you could try the extremes first).  Look into the mvrnorm() function in the MASS package for random multivariate-normal draws.

I'm not even sure about the validity of the test you want to perform, so you might want to post your question on SEMNET and see if any more informed researchers have better advice:

http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html
